newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar likely to face mild retreat, economists say.
newsitem.headline: Dollar likely to face mild retreat, economists say.

text.p: The dollar is likely to retreat mildly against the yen by the end of the current fiscal year, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Thursday.
The average of the forecasts made by 25 economists put the dollar at 110.61 yen by the end of 1996 and 109.04 yen at the end of the current business year next March.
Economists at 30 banks, securities firms and research institutions in Tokyo and London were polled on October 15-17 on the Japanese economy but not all responded to all the questions.
Some of the economists predicted the dollar could hit a peak of about 115 yen by the end of December before falling.

"The dollar could slide mildly to around 108 by the end of March next year after enjoying a further advance to around 115 yen over the next few months," said Mamoru Yamazaki, senior economist at Paribas Capital Markets.
The dollar stood at around 112.80 on Thursday after reaching a 33-month high of 113.10 yen on Wednesday in New York.
A booming investment spree in foreign securities by Japanese investors in pursuit of higher returns has increased the downward pressure on the yen against major currencies.

The investors have been forced overseas because of record low interest rates in Japan, and economists are convinced the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will keep its easy monetary policy to help safeguard the economic recovery, especially after the pro-business, conservative Liberal Democratic Party boosted its strength in last Sunday's general election. The LDP is expected to emphasise the need to nurture the fragile recovery.

The central bank has also been forced to cling to its current record low interest rate of 0.5 percent because of the sluggish Tokyo stock market, said Hideki Naito, managing analyst at MMS International.
The only risk of a dollar fall in the near term may come after the U.S. presidential election on November 5.
"There is a risk of the yen rising once the U.S. election is over," said Paribas' Yamazaki.

The economists said the dollar may lose ground if market participants start to feel that stabilising U.S. financial markets through a strong dollar was no longer in the best interests of the Clinton administration.

The United States may instead start taking a tough stance against Japan over trade and financial disputes, giving rise to speculation Washington could use exchange rates as a tool to get concessions from Japan.
U.S. exporters have already voiced concerns about the dollar's rise to 110 yen undermining their competitiveness abroad.
"However, such risks would be smaller than before, since China has replaced Japan as the country with the biggest trade surplus with the U.S.," Yamazaki added.
Changes in the fundamental factors pointing to a yen rise are expected to surface sometime early next year, the economists said.

The biggest factors for a mild dollar retreat are expectations that the U.S.-Japan trade imbalance will stop improving after a year of shrinkage, and that the interest rate gap between the nations will not expand further.
"A slowdown in Japan's import volume, which is currently being shrugged off in the market, may draw fresh attention," said Takashi Masuda, a senior economist at NCB Research Institute.

Also, expectations are likely to emerge around next March that interest rates in Japan will rise, said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at Industrial Bank of Japan, adding that the United States was likely to face a slowdown in its economy and thus interest rates there would decline.
